messages.subject: unconditional simulation of spde model
messages.body_plain:
Hi there!

As a simple excercise, I have modified the leuk.demo.R code and tried to
perform unconditional simulation of Matï¿½rn GMRFs on the unit square.
However, I get a discrepancy between the theoretical and the empirical
correlations.
I can't see where is the mistake, may be you can.

Here is the code. Thanks in advance!
ï¿½acu.-

##########################################
### Unconditional sample on the square ###
##########################################
library(INLA)

# Prediction locations
unit.sq <- matrix(c(0,1,1,0,0,0,1,1), ncol=2)
mesh = inla.mesh.create(boundary=inla.mesh.segment(unit.sq),
refine=list(max.edge=0.06))

## Create the SPDE/GMRF model, (kappa^2-Delta)(tau x) = W:
spde = inla.spde.create(mesh, model="matern", param=list(alpha=2))

## Calculate mapping between triangulation vertices and grid points:
proj = inla.mesh.projector(mesh, dims=c(200,200))

## Parameters
range <- .8
var <- 1
kappa <- sqrt(8)/range
tau <- 1/sqrt(4*pi*kappa(range)^2*var)

## Get unconditional sample and precision matrix
sample <- inla.spde.query(spde, sample=list(tau=tau, kappa2=kappa^2),
precision=list(tau=tau, kappa2=kappa^2))

## Calculate covariances (S) and correlations (SS):
Q <- sample$precision
S <- solve(Q) # covariance matrix
SS <- diag(1/sqrt(diag(S))) %*% S %*% diag(1/sqrt(diag(S))) #
correlation matrix

## Reference point for covariance/correlation comparisons:
ref.s = (which.min((mesh$loc[,1]-mean(range(mesh$loc[,1])))^2 +
(mesh$loc[,2]-mean(range(mesh$loc[,2])))^2))

## Theoretical Matern correlations and covariances:
dd = (0:1000)/1000
SS.theory = (dd*kappa)*besselK(dd*kappa,1)
SS.theory[1] = 1
S.theory = SS.theory/(4*pi*kappa^2)/tau^2

## Compare correlations
D = as.matrix(dist(mesh$loc))
plot(D[ref.s,],SS[ref.s,],type="p",pch=20,
xlab="Distance",ylab="Correlation",
xlim=c(0.0,1.0),ylim=c(-0.005,1.005))
lines(dd,SS.theory,type="l",
col=rgb(0.5,0.5,0.5),lwd=2)

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Your correlation range is almost as long as the width of your domain.  As shown in Appendix A.4, the effect of the Neumann boundary conditions is visible within at least the distance of the range away from the boundary, which in this example is the entire domain.  (We're working on other boundary conditions that will reduce or eliminate this effect.)

The easiest workaround is to extend the representation domain, to move the boundary effect outside the region of interest.  See the attached file for a modified version of your example that does this (as well as alternate ways of computing the reference covariances, etc.).

/Finn

messages.subject_clean: Using data with weights similar to the use in the standard glm function in R
messages.body_plain:
I would like to analyse biologic responses with genotypes using the INLA
package in R. My special intention is to include individuals, experiment
days and
individual ages as random variables (using iid and random-walk models).
The problem I have is that my genetic data contain an uncertainty parameter.
This means, that I have a table looking like this:

  Individual    Response (always the same)            Genotype
Probability (sum up to 1 per individual)    Age    Day of Experiment
Sex etc.
  1                0.3
    A                    0.2
  1                0.3
    B                    0.1
  1                0.3
    C                    0.8

With glm models in R, it is always possible to include the "Probability"
in a "weights" vector for the observations.
Is there a similar way to do it with inla?

I have a similar problem with an association study, where I would like
to include age as a random walk. How can I add "weights". I did not find
an answer in the FAQ or the documentation. But maybe there is a trick
for that? Or can I write a likelihood function by myself which would include
weights?

Best regards from Lübeck,
Andreas

messages.body_plain:
Andreas,

On Dec 8, 2:17 pm, Andreas Recke <Andreas.Re...@uk-sh.de> wrote:
> ... The problem I have is that my genetic data contain an uncertainty parameter.

> This means, that I have a table looking like this:
>
>   Individual    Response (always the same)            Genotype
> Probability (sum up to 1 per individual)    Age    Day of Experiment    Sex
> etc.

>  id y G Pr ...
>   1 0.3 A 0.2 ...
>   1 0.3 B 0.1 ...
>   1 0.3 C 0.8 ...

I reorganized the above table to understand your data. I guess the
last 0.8 needs to be 0.7. Are genotype levels A, B, and C actually
genotypes of one locus, e.g., A=AA, B=AB, and C=BB? If yes, then you
can not say that you have three y records per one individual. You have
one y record, but uncertainty in genotype. If you want to fit a model
to infer the effect of genotype on phenotype then you can fit it with
data being organized as:

id y GAA GAB GBB ...
1 0.3 0.2 0.1 0.7 --> uncertain genotype information
2 0.8 1.0 0.0 0.0 --> this individual has certainly genotype AA
3 0.9 0.0 1.0 0.0 --> this individual has certainly genotype AB
3 1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 --> this individual has certainly genotype BB

and in the model you simply have three covariates

y ~ GAA + GAB + GBB

where the estimate of regression coefficients of y on each G* would
represent genotype effects. If you are willing to assume only additive
effect at this locus you can do

GC <- with(mydata, GAA*0 + GAB*1 + GBB*2)

y ~ GC

where the estimate of regression coefficient of y on GC would be the
average allele substitution effect.

Regards, Gregor Gorjanc

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 2011-12-14 at 11:25 +0100, Facundo Muñoz wrote:
> Hi there!
>
> I'm fitting a glmm with INLA, using the temperature as a covariate for a
> fixed effect.
> The problem is that I only have temperature data on a set of
> meteorological stations, so I need to infer the temperature for the rest
> of the territory.
>
> The first simple approach would be to perform some kind of
> interpolation, and use it as the covariate.
> Of course I would like to take the prediction error into account, so I'm
> trying to address this with INLA.
>
> I first thought in fitting a spatial model for the temperature using the
> spde module.
> But I don't see how to include the result in the linear predictor of the
> glmm.
>
> The right full bayesian approach would be to fit both the temperature
> and the response variable of the glmm at the same time.
>
> Is this possible?
>
> Thanks! (again)

> ƒacu.-
>

yes. the joint for the responce and the temperature field is Gaussian,
conditioned on the hyperparams.

case 1.

temperature is exactly observed. then this is just

	y ~ 1 + f(idx1, `spde1') + f(idx, `spde2')

with obvious notation. except for two issues. first, you know some of
the f(idx1)'s, which you can fix, adding a second Gaussian likelihood
with high fixed precision, so that

	f(idx1, `spde1') = temperature.observed.

for those 'idx1' where its observed. second issue, is that the formula
above, does set the 'fixed effect coefficient' beta.temperature to 1. to
avoid this, use the copy feature,

http://www.r-inla.org/models/tools#TOC-Copying-a-model

which has a such scaling but its default = 1 and fixed. so

y ~ 1 + f(idx1, `spde1') + f(idx1.copy, copy="idx1", fixed=FALSE) +
f(idx, `spde2')

will estimate a scaling of the temperature model. then set 'idx1' = NA
where idx1.copy is not NA. so only one is active at the time.

case 2.

if the temperature is observed with noise, then this is the same as case
1, except that the precision for the temperature is unknown.

I think that's it. I hope you can decode the sketch given above...

--

messages.subject: Re: inla.fmesher.smorg
messages.body_plain:
The fmesher program used by inla.mesh.create only knows how to generate triangulations on planes and spheres, but the code for constructing SPDE models can handle any 2-manifold. The general manifolds we've shown were generated by deforming spherical meshes, either through radial deformation based on a random field generated on the sphere (via SPDE/GMRF) or as a full 3-variate SPDE/GMRF on the sphere.

Triangulations generated by other programs, or by hand can be translated into inla.mesh format by supplying both tv and loc to inla.mesh.create, where tv is a matrix of vertex indices for each triangle, in count clockwise order, and loc is a matrix of vertex coordinates, in R3.
For example, it should be possible to use the CGAL library to generate triangulationstand use with inla, but I haven't tried that.

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

This is due to a lack of storage-mode-checking by inla.mesh.create.  The following modification should work:

mtest <- inla.mesh.create(loc=matrix(c(0,1,2,3,0,2,1,0), ncol=2), tv=matrix(as.integer(c(2,3,1,1,3,4)), ncol=3), extend=FALSE)

I'll add code to the package to make sure it gives fmesher an interger matrix for tv.  Thanks for the test cases...

Note:
When "tv" is supplied, "extend" defaults to FALSE, and fmesher doesn't actually honor "extend=TRUE" when given a full triangulation; the effect could instead be mimicked by constructing lots of "interior segments".  The only other current situation where extend=FALSE works is when a lattice or explicit boundaries are supplied; we've found a way of extending that to arbitrary planar point sets, but haven't implemented that in the package yet.

messages.subject_clean: BYM model with covariate: how to obtain the excess deaths across all areas?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am doing an BYM ecological model with a covariate (X_i), i.e.

O_i ~ Poisson(mu_i)
Log(mu_i) = log(E_i) + a + b*X_i + S_i +H_i
Where O_i is the observed mortality

And I would like to calculate the excess deaths in the i-th area = Ô_i – Ô’_i where Ô_i is the posterior predictive value of observed deaths in the i-th  area and Ô’_i the posterior predictive value of expected deaths in the i-th area if X_i has known values =z_i

I would like to obtain
Ô_i ~ Poisson(mu_i) where mu_i=exp(log(E_i) + a + b*X_i + S_i +H_i)
Ô’_i ~ Poisson(mu’_i) where mu’_i=exp(log(E_i) + a + b*z_i + S_i +H_i)

And finally obtain the excess of death by summing the excess deaths (Ô_i – Ô’_i) across all areas.

  With INLA I can predict and obtain the posterior distributions of Ô_i and Ô’_i. But I don’t know if it would be possible obtain de posterior distribution of Ô_i – Ô’_i for each area. And finally the posterior distribution of the sum of Ô_i – Ô’_I across all the areas. Moreover, I’m interested in obtaining the credible intervals of this excess number of deaths.

  Can anyone help me??

Thank you very much!

Marc

what you get is to get the marginal for log(O_i) - log(O_j), and also
the posterior correlation matrix better log(O_i) and log(O_j).

having the marginal for log(O_i) and log(O_j) and the correlation
between log(O_i) and log(O_j), cries out for a Gaussian copula with
these marginals and correlation, then you have the joint (approx) for
O_i and O_j; see
